text: About twenty-seven million people came through the gates that season.
On a single day in October, called Chicago Day, the fair drew more than seven hundred and fifty thousand, a record for an outdoor event.
And while those crowds moved through the White City, a small group of Black Americans set out to tell them what the fair was leaving out.
The organizers had refused to give African Americans any real part in planning the exposition.
There was no building, no commission, no place at the table.
Wells, the anti-lynching journalist, had a different plan.
A year earlier, her newspaper office in Memphis had been destroyed by a mob after she wrote about the lynching of three Black grocers, and she had been driven out of the South.
She came to the fair carrying that story.
With Frederick Douglass, the educator Irvine Garland Penn, and the lawyer Ferdinand Barnett, who would later become her husband, she put together a pamphlet.
They called it The Reason Why the Colored American Is Not in the World's Columbian Exposition.
It came out on the thirtieth of August.
It ran through the achievements of Black Americans in the thirty years since slavery had ended.
It also laid out the convict-lease system, the laws stripping the vote, and the lynchings spreading across the South, with names and numbers.
The fair told a story of progress.
The pamphlet told the other half of it.
